pageTitles.home: LabML — machine learning in your browser

about.title: How it works — and why your data is safe.
about.lede: LabML is a machine learning lab that runs entirely in your browser. This page explains the engine, and how each design choice keeps your data on your machine.

how.title: How it works
how.body: Your CSV is parsed in a Web Worker inside this tab. The lab profiles every column, detects the task from your target, then holds back 20% of the rows (seeded, stratified) before fitting anything — imputation, encoding and scaling are learned on the training split only, so the test score is honest. Six models train in the worker and land on a live leaderboard, always compared to a naive baseline. Insights (confusion matrix, ROC, permutation importance, what-if) interrogate the real trained models kept in worker memory.

local.title: Read locally, provably
local.body: The file never leaves the tab. Open your browser's Network panel and run a full training: no requests go out. The Content-Security-Policy of this site forbids third-party calls altogether — that is the proof, not a promise.

storage.title: History stays here
storage.body: Saved runs live in your browser's IndexedDB — metrics and charts only, never the source rows. Delete them anytime; nothing exists anywhere else.

share.title: Data-free sharing
share.body: Share links compress the run's metrics into the URL fragment — the part after # that browsers never send to any server. Your correspondent sees the results, not your data.

offline.title: Works offline
offline.body: LabML is an installable PWA: once loaded, cut the Wi-Fi and everything — demo datasets included — still works. Hard to exfiltrate data without a network.

openSource.title: Under the hood
openSource.body: The entire lab — parsing, models, metrics — is hand-written and covered by automated tests (unit, end-to-end, accessibility). No external ML service, no CDN: everything ships with the app.

privacy.title: Your data never leaves your browser
privacy.lede: This is not a privacy policy written by lawyers: it is a technical property of the application, and you can check it yourself in two minutes without taking our word for anything.

promise.title: The promise, plainly
promise.body: When you drop a file into LabML, your browser reads it and it stays in the tab's memory. No row, no column, no file name, no question you ask the assistant, no webcam frame is sent to a server — not ours, not anyone's. There is no account, no upload, no tracker, no analytics, no automatic error reporting.

how.title: How it is enforced — not merely claimed

csp.title: The browser blocks leaks itself
csp.body: The site is served with a strict Content-Security-Policy whose connect-src 'self' directive allows no connection to any other domain. This is not our code politely restraining itself: your browser would refuse the request even if the code tried to make it.

assets.title: Everything is self-hosted
assets.body: No third-party script, no CDN font, no remote image, no widget. The vision models, the ONNX runtime and the language-model weights all come from our own domain — which is why they show up in the Network tab, and why they are all that shows up.

workers.title: The computing happens in Web Workers
workers.body: Parsing, cleaning, training, predictions, questions to the assistant: all of it runs in threads belonging to your tab. Your data travels between the page and its workers, never outward.

storage.title: Nothing is kept without a click from you
storage.body: By default, closing the tab erases everything. A dataset is stored — in IndexedDB, on your own disk, nowhere else — only if you explicitly click « keep », and the « forget » button deletes it.

header.title: The header actually served
header.body: Here is the security policy returned with every page of this site. You do not have to believe us: the Network tab shows it to you, and this block is checked against the real configuration file on every build.
header.note: This is the line that matters — it forbids any request to another domain:
header.camera: And for the Vision module's webcam, the camera is allowed for this site only, never for a third-party frame:

verify.title: Check it yourself
verify.lede: Four checks, from quickest to most convincing. None of them depends on our word or on our code.

offline.title: Cut the network
offline.body: The shortest test, and the hardest to fake. Open the developer tools (F12, or ⌥⌘I on Mac), Network tab, switch the « No throttling » menu to « Offline » — or simply turn off Wi-Fi. Reload the page, drop a CSV, train a model, ask a question. Everything still works. An application that ships your data elsewhere to process it could not.

network.title: Watch the Network tab while you work
network.body: Developer tools → Network. Tick « Preserve log », clear the list, then drop your file and start a training run. Filter on Fetch/XHR: nothing happens. Your file is not transmitted, because there is nobody to transmit it to.

headers.title: Read the security policy at the source
headers.body: Still in Network, click the first row — the HTML document — then « Headers » → « Response Headers ». Look for Content-Security-Policy and the connect-src 'self' part. It is the very string shown above on this page.

storage.title: Open local storage
storage.body: Application tab → IndexedDB → labml. You see exactly what you chose to keep: your past runs, and your datasets only if you asked for them. The Data Studio's « forget » button empties that database in front of you.

figure.title: What you should see
figure.emptyNote: Nothing further while you load a file and train
figure.calloutEmpty: the only rows are the application's own files, served by our domain
figure.caption: Diagram of the Network tab — labels differ between browsers and languages. This is not a capture of your screen: it is what you should find there.
figure.alt: Diagram of the developer tools Network tab: a few application files, the Offline selector highlighted, and no request while you work.

live.title: Live proof, in your own browser
live.body: This panel reads this page's resource timeline — the same one the Network tab displays — and counts the requests per domain.
live.clean: {{total}} requests, all to {{origin}}. None to a third party.
live.caveat: Honesty about this panel: it reads our own timeline, so it is a convenience, not the final proof. Requests made inside a Web Worker have their own timeline and do not appear here, and a request blocked by the security policy never appears at all. The real proof is the four checks above: they do not go through our code.

traffic.title: What actually travels over the network
traffic.body: For the sake of precision, here is the complete list. All of it comes from our domain, and none of it starts without an action from you:
traffic.app: the application's own files (HTML, JavaScript, styles, fonts), on first load, then cached for offline use;
traffic.demo: the demo datasets, only if you click one of them;
traffic.vision: the vision models, only when you open the Vision module;
traffic.llm: the local language model's weights, only if you explicitly accept the download.
traffic.never: What never travels: your file, its name, your columns, your values, your questions, your results, your webcam frames. No analytics, no account, no cookie, no error report.

home.lede: Drop a dataset, pick what to predict, and train a set of models on your own machine. No account, no upload, no setup — and every run is scored against an honest baseline.

ml.title: ML Lab

home.statusBody: The three modules are live: the ML Lab (training, insights, export, offline PWA), AI vision (on-device image classification) and the Data Studio (quality report, cleaning, hand-off to the lab).

ml.titlePre: From a CSV to a leaderboard,
ml.titleHighlight: without your data leaving the tab.
ml.lede: The lab reads your file locally, works out the task, trains a set of models and holds back part of the data to test them honestly.

upload.title: Drop a dataset
upload.description: Drag in a CSV — it is read right here in the browser, nothing is sent anywhere.

target.title: Pick a target
target.description: Choose the column to predict; the lab suggests which columns to keep.

train.title: Train models
train.description: One click. Several models are trained in parallel workers, with live progress.

read.title: Read the results
read.description: Leaderboard, metrics against a naive baseline, plots, top features and a plain read.

lab.title: new run
lab.dropTitle: Drop a CSV or Excel file
lab.dropHint: or click to browse — the file is read right here in your browser, nothing is uploaded
lab.errorBody: The file looks empty or not tabular. Try a CSV with a header row.
lab.errorTooLargeTitle: File too large for browser memory
lab.errorTooLarge: This file exceeds the {{max}}-cell budget (rows × columns) the lab holds in memory — reading stopped, on purpose, at {{rows}} rows × {{cols}} columns. Split the file or drop columns, then try again.
lab.errorDatasetMissingTitle: This dataset is no longer in this browser
lab.errorDatasetMissing: It had been kept here, but local storage no longer holds it — it was forgotten, or the browser cleared its site data. Nothing was misread: drop the file again to carry on.

unsupported.type: This column cannot be a target — pick a numeric or categorical column.
unsupported.tooManyClasses: Too many distinct classes for a target — pick a column with at most 20.

lab.leakAlert: Target leakage: {{columns}} almost perfectly mirrors the target — excluded automatically.
lab.trainConfig: seed {{seed}} · split {{split}} · trained in your browser
lab.reproducibleNote: Same data, same seed, same results — every run is reproducible by construction.

leaderboard.runInfo: seed {{seed}} · {{train}} train rows · {{test}} test rows · {{features}} features after encoding
leaderboard.skipped: skipped (dates and identifiers are not features): {{columns}}
leaderboard.trainedOnTitle: Trained on an announced seeded sample of {{rows}} of the {{total}} training rows — never silently. The score comes from the same full test set as every other model.
leaderboard.sampledFrom: announced sample: {{cap}} of {{from}} usable rows (seeded, stratified)
leaderboard.testTitle: The score on the reporting split — held out from selection. It is the number to quote.
leaderboard.championLine: {{model}} was selected on validation at {{val}} and scores {{test}} on the untouched test set ({{gap}}).
leaderboard.championWhy: Selecting the best of several models on a split makes that split optimistic — reporting on a third, never-selected split is what keeps the headline number honest.
leaderboard.runInfoVal: seed {{seed}} · {{train}} train rows · {{val}} validation rows · {{test}} test rows · {{features}} features after encoding
leaderboard.splitChronological: chronological split on {{column}} (oldest rows train, newest test)
leaderboard.splitGroup: grouped split on {{column}} (no group on both sides)
leaderboard.leakWarning: « {{column}} » alone predicts the target at {{score}}% on the validation split.
leaderboard.leakAdvice: A single column reading the target that well is almost always leakage — information that would not exist at prediction time. Exclude it and retrain, or confirm it is legitimately available.
leaderboard.ensembleNote: Ensemble: the average of {{members}} — already trained, so it costs nothing more. The baseline is never a member.
leaderboard.weighting: class weighting: balanced ({{loss}} weight the loss, {{resample}} use a seeded balanced resample)
leaderboard.imbalanceHint: The largest class holds {{share}}% of the training rows. Accuracy rewards always answering it — rank on F1 or recall, and try class weighting.
leaderboard.weightToggleHint: Weights the training loss (logistic regression, gradient boosting) or resamples the rows (tree, forest) so the rare class counts as much as the common one.

forecast.title: Time series
forecast.hint: This dataset carries a date column. The lab can forecast a numeric value over time: naive, seasonal naive, exponential smoothing (SES, Holt, additive Holt-Winters — hand-written), the winner picked by a rolling-origin backtest that never peeks at the future.
forecast.summary: {{points}} points ({{freq}}) · backtest on the last {{holdout}} points · winner: {{winner}} with MAE {{mae}} (naive: {{naive}}).
forecast.note: The band is the empirical 80% interval of the winner's one-step backtest errors — measured, not assumed. Every method was scored on forecasts made strictly before each held-out point.

explore.title: Explore without a target
explore.hint: No column to predict? The lab can group similar rows on its own: seeded k-means (k = 2–5, chosen by silhouette) on the same encoded features, projected in 2D by PCA — hand-written, deterministic, in your browser.
explore.summary: {{k}} groups · silhouette {{silhouette}} (tried k = {{tried}}) · {{rows}} rows · the two PCA axes carry {{p1}} % + {{p2}} % of the variance
explore.note: Groups are a reading aid, not a ground truth: k-means favors roundish groups of similar size. Same data, same seed — same groups, always.

tuning.title: Hyperparameter search
tuning.hint: Seeded random search: up to {{budget}} configurations scored by {{folds}}-fold cross-validation on the training split only — the held-out test set is scored exactly once, at the end.
tuning.note: The winner is chosen by cross-validation, never by peeking at the test set — so the test delta can be negative. That is honest evaluation, not a bug.
tuning.sampled: Search ran on an announced seeded sample of {{rows}} of {{from}} training rows — the same rows the leaderboard model trained on.

curve.title: Would more data help?
curve.hint: The learning curve retrains one model on growing seeded fractions of the training split — the same nested samples the announced caps use — and scores each size on the same full test set, with a 95% bootstrap band. If the curve is still climbing at the right edge, collecting more rows is worth it; if it is flat, work on features or the model instead.
curve.refused: No curve here: the dataset offers a single training size (or the model is the flat-by-definition baseline).
curve.axis: {{model}} — {{metric}} vs training rows · every point scored on the same {{test}} test rows
curve.climbing: The curve is still climbing: the last step ({{from}} → {{to}} rows) gains {{gain}} [{{lo}} ; {{hi}}], and the gain survives resampling. More data would probably help this model.
curve.plateau: The curve has flattened: the last step ({{from}} → {{to}} rows) shows no decisive gain ({{gain}}). Collecting more rows is probably not the priority — work on features or the model instead.
curve.capCost: The curve stops at the announced {{cap}}-row training cap — and it was still climbing there, so the cap costs this model some accuracy.
curve.capFree: The curve stops at the announced {{cap}}-row training cap — it had already flattened, so the cap costs nothing here.
curve.note: Each point retrains from scratch on a seeded nested prefix of the {{trainRows}} training rows (smaller sizes are subsets of larger ones) and the pipeline is refitted on that prefix only. The band is the 95% bootstrap interval on the test draw — sensitivity to the test set, not training variance. The verdict judges only the last size step.

batch.title: Score a new batch
batch.hint: The production gesture: drop a new file and {{model}} scores it right here — predictions for every row, and if the file carries the target column, an honest comparison against the held-out test set. Nothing is uploaded.
batch.missingColumns: This file is missing feature columns the model needs: {{list}}.
batch.error: This file could not be scored ({{detail}}).
batch.unknownLabels_one: {{count}} row carries a label never seen in training — predicted, but kept out of the metrics.
batch.unknownLabels_other: {{count}} rows carry labels never seen in training — predicted, but kept out of the metrics.
batch.noTarget: No target column in this file — predictions only, no metrics to compare.
batch.note: A drop against the test set is a signal, not a bug: the world moved. Check the input drift in the Data Studio (PSI) to see which columns shifted.

threshold.title: Decision threshold & imbalance
threshold.hint: Only {{rate}} % of rows are “{{positive}}”: accuracy flatters any model here. The precision-recall curve tells the truth, the calibration curve says whether the probabilities can be trusted — and the threshold is YOUR decision, priced by your costs.
threshold.note: A probability is not a decision. Above the threshold the row is flagged “positive” — moving it trades false alarms against missed cases, and the right trade depends on what each mistake costs YOU. The dot on the curve is your current choice; it is saved with the run.
threshold.oneVsRestNote: One-vs-rest: this reads how well the model separates « {{class}} » from every other class. It is not a complete multiclass decision rule — two classes can both clear their thresholds, and nothing here says which would win.

segments.title: Where the model fails
segments.hint: The test set ({{rows}} rows) is sliced by each categorical column — including columns kept out of the features, where proxy effects can hide. Slices with fewer than {{min}} test rows are excluded.
segments.small_one: {{count}} slice with fewer than {{min}} test rows excluded.
segments.small_other: {{count}} slices with fewer than {{min}} test rows excluded.
segments.note: A gap is a finding to investigate, not a verdict — a small slice moves for one hard row as easily as for a real weakness. A gap on a column outside the features means the model reaches it through proxies.

uncertainty.title: How solid are these numbers?
uncertainty.hint: The test set ({{rows}} rows) is bootstrap-resampled and each model's {{metric}} is recomputed every time — the interval is where the metric lands 95 times out of 100. A wide interval is information, not a defect.
uncertainty.verdictReal: {{winner}} beats {{against}}: Δ {{metric}} = {{delta}} [{{lo}} ; {{hi}}] — the gap survives resampling ({{share}}% of resamples). Probably real.
uncertainty.verdictNoise: {{winner}} vs {{against}}: Δ {{metric}} = {{delta}} [{{lo}} ; {{hi}}] — the interval crosses zero. Possibly noise: on this test set, the winner is not proven better.
uncertainty.note: Resamples are drawn from the same {{rows}} test rows (seed {{seed}}, shared across models so comparisons are paired). These intervals measure sensitivity to the test draw — not training variance.

compare.title: Run comparison
compare.notComparable: These runs predict different things — the metrics do not compare. The configuration diff below still tells the story.
compare.read: The best model goes from {{aPrimary}} ({{aModel}}) to {{bPrimary}} ({{bModel}}) — {{metric}} {{delta}}.
compare.sameFeatures: Both runs trained on the same features.
compare.intervalsDisjoint: The intervals do not overlap — the gap between the two runs exceeds both uncertainties. Probably real.
compare.intervalsOverlap: The intervals overlap — on these test sets, the gap between the two runs could be noise.
compare.intervalsNote: Each interval comes from its own run's test draw (v20). Two runs are never paired — read this as an indication, not a test.
compare.manyHint: Every run is read against {{reference}}, the oldest of the selection — so the deltas say what your changes did, not what the newest run happens to be.
compare.manyIncomparable: These runs do not predict the same thing — the numbers are shown, but they are not deltas. Read each column on its own.
compare.manyMissing: Not enough runs to compare — select between 2 and 6 saved runs from the lab history.

imported.title: Reuse an exported model
imported.hint: Trained here before? Drop the exported model (.json) — it scores new files without retraining. Everything stays in your browser.
imported.scoreCta: Score a CSV with this model
imported.scoreHint: The file must carry the feature columns above; a target column is optional and only feeds the honest comparison.
imported.note: The reference column is the exporting run's held-out test — a different draw than this file. Read gaps as signals, not verdicts.

errors.invalid-json: This file is not valid JSON.
errors.not-labml: This JSON was not exported by LabML.
errors.unsupported-version: Format v{{detail}} predates re-import — export the model again from a fresh run.
errors.bad-manifest: The manifest is incomplete — this export cannot be trusted to predict.
errors.unsupported-kind: Unknown model family in this export.
errors.missingColumns: The file is missing required columns: {{detail}}.
errors.generic: The file could not be processed.

datasets.listNote: Stored locally in IndexedDB (compressed) — nothing ever leaves your machine, and share links never carry data.
datasets.quotaError: Does not fit: this file needs {{needed}} but {{used}} of the {{quota}} budget are in use. Forget a dataset below to make room.

insights.title: Insights
insights.selectHint: Click any leaderboard row to inspect another model.
insights.importanceHintClassification: Accuracy drop when the column is shuffled (permutation importance, model-agnostic).
insights.importanceHintRegression: RMSE increase when the column is shuffled (permutation importance, model-agnostic).
insights.readAccuracy: {{model}} gets {{accuracy}}% of the {{rows}} held-out test rows right.
insights.readBaseline: That is {{delta}} points above the naive baseline ({{baseline}}%), so the model has learned real signal.
insights.readRecall: It catches {{recall}}% of the actual "{{label}}" cases.
insights.readRegression: {{model}}'s predictions are off by {{mae}} on average across the {{rows}} held-out test rows.
insights.readVariance: It explains {{r2}}% of the variance of the target.
insights.pdpHint: Average model prediction as this column sweeps its range, everything else unchanged.
insights.whatIfHint: Edit the values and watch the model's live prediction — computed locally, like everything else.
insights.explainTitle: What pushes the value up or down, versus a typical row
insights.explainTitleClass: What pushes toward or away from “{{class}}”, versus a typical row
insights.explainNote: Shapley values estimated by permutation sampling ({{permutations}} permutations × {{references}} reference rows, seeded). The bars sum exactly to the gap between this prediction and the reference average.
insights.wordsHintClassification: Average shift of the predicted probability of “{{class}}” when the word is erased from the reviews containing it — right pushes up, left pushes down.
insights.wordsHintRegression: Average shift of the prediction when the word is erased from the texts containing it — right pushes up, left pushes down.
insights.wordsNote: One word at a time, on the held-out test rows. A review says the same thing several ways, so erasing one word rarely flips a prediction on its own.
insights.wordsSaturated: This model cannot answer the word question: its probabilities are saturated — it returns almost only 0 or 1 — so erasing a word shifts the answer by exactly zero.
insights.wordsSaturatedAdvice: That is a property of the model, not of the words. Pick another model in the leaderboard (logistic regression and gradient boosting give graded probabilities) to read the word effects.

export.knnNote: k-NN cannot be exported — it memorizes the training data.

runs.title: Run history
runs.note: Stored in your browser (IndexedDB) — metrics only, never your data.
runs.empty: No runs yet — train some models above.

runArtifacts.hint: These analyses were run after training and saved with the run — they travel with the local history, the HTML report and share links, never with the data.

share.note: This link carries only metrics and charts — never the original data. It lives in the URL fragment, which browsers do not send to any server.

lab.reportFooter: Generated locally by LabML — no data ever left the browser.

robust.title: Is this ranking real?
robust.hint: A single split ranks on one draw of a few hundred rows, and two models a point apart can swap places on the next draw. This retrains every family on 5 repetitions × 2 halves of the training and validation rows — ten fits each — and reports a mean, a spread, and how often the leader actually beat the runner-up. The test set stays out of the folds: this re-ranks, it does not re-test.
robust.verdictStable: {{leader}} beat {{runnerUp}} in {{wins}} of {{folds}} folds — the order between them is stable.
robust.verdictNoise: {{leader}} beat {{runnerUp}} in only {{wins}} of {{folds}} folds — the order between them is inside the noise, so treat them as tied.
robust.note: {{folds}} folds ({{reps}} repetitions × 2 halves) over {{rows}} training and validation rows. The pipeline is refitted inside every fold; the test set is never touched.

read.title: How this file was read
read.encodingFallback: Encoding: windows-1252 — UTF-8 decoding failed on these bytes, so this is a certainty, not a preference. Accents would otherwise have come through as replacement characters.
read.decimal_one: Decimal comma detected and converted in {{count}} column: {{columns}}. The figure in brackets is how many values proved it.
read.decimal_other: Decimal comma detected and converted in {{count}} columns: {{columns}}. The figure in brackets is how many values proved it.
read.grouped: Thousands separators were removed as well.
read.renamed_one: {{count}} column was renamed so that every name means exactly one column: {{columns}}. A repeated name otherwise resolved to a different column depending on which part of the code looked it up.
read.renamed_other: {{count}} columns were renamed so that every name means exactly one column: {{columns}}. A repeated name otherwise resolved to a different column depending on which part of the code looked it up.
read.malformed_one: {{count}} row did not match what the file declares: an unclosed quote, or a cell count that differs from the column count. It was read as best it could be — extra cells dropped, missing cells left empty — and it is reported here rather than lost in silence.
read.malformed_other: {{count}} rows did not match what the file declares: an unclosed quote, or a cell count that differs from the column count. They were read as best they could be — extra cells dropped, missing cells left empty — and they are reported here rather than lost in silence.
read.hint: A column is only rewritten when nearly all of its values are numbers in that format and it would otherwise not be numeric at all. Anything else is left exactly as written. If this reading is wrong, reload the file — the detection is per column, not per file.

data.title: Diagnose and clean a dataset, without uploading it.
data.lede: Drop a file: the studio measures its quality — missing values, duplicates, inconsistent spellings, outliers — then repairs it with a transparent recipe. Entirely in your browser, like the rest of LabML.

drop.title: Drop a CSV or Excel file
drop.hint: or click to browse — .csv, .tsv, .xlsx. Read locally in a Web Worker, never uploaded.

data.error: This file could not be read ({{detail}}). Try a CSV, TSV or Excel file with a header row.

join.title: Join a second file
join.hint: Enrich {{name}} with columns from another file, matched on a shared key column. Matching is exact after trimming — a messy key shows up as an orphan, not silently. The joined result becomes THE dataset: quality report, recipe, drift and the ML Lab all continue from it.
join.noKey: No column name in common between the two files — the key must exist on both sides.
join.verdict: {{other}} joined on “{{key}}”: {{matched}} of {{total}} rows matched, {{columns}} columns added.
join.orphans_one: {{count}} row found no match — unmatched key: {{keys}}.
join.orphans_other: {{count}} rows found no match — unmatched keys: {{keys}}.
join.duplicates_one: {{count}} duplicated key on the joined file (first occurrence wins).
join.duplicates_other: {{count}} duplicated keys on the joined file (first occurrence wins).
join.unused_one: {{count}} row of the joined file matched nothing.
join.unused_other: {{count}} rows of the joined file matched nothing.
join.note: Left join: every original row survives; unmatched rows keep empty new columns. Orphans caused by messy keys (case, spaces) are a cleaning finding — merge the variants in the recipe below.

score.breakdownHint: Each part carries its own weight and the points it actually cost. The weights sum to 105, not 100: validity brought its own 5 points in V40 rather than taking them from an existing part, so a file with no impossible values scores exactly what it scored before.

issues.title: What the studio found
issues.none: Nothing to report: no missing cells, duplicates, spelling variants or outliers. This dataset is ready.

missing.body: Empty cells and tokens like “NA” or “?”. Models cannot use them as-is: fill them or drop the rows.

duplicates.body: Rows identical to an earlier row. They double-count observations and can leak between train and test splits.

messy.body: The same category written several ways (case, stray spaces). Left as-is, each spelling counts as a different category.

outliers.body: Values outside the Tukey fences (1.5 × IQR) of their column — often typos or unit mix-ups. Check before clamping.

structural.body: Constant or near-empty columns carry no signal; identifiers are flagged for information and never dropped automatically.

validity.body: Present, correctly typed, and still impossible. Flagged, never repaired — the recipe is where data changes.

consistency.body: Every cell is fine; the row is not. Two columns disagree with each other.

rules.dateOrder: {{columns}}: the end comes before the start
rules.productMismatch: {{columns}}: the total is not quantity × price

recipe.title: Cleaning recipe
recipe.importError: This file is not a LabML recipe.
recipe.typesHint: Force how a column is treated by the cleaning steps (variant merging, imputation, outlier clamping, date expansion). “Auto” keeps the inferred type.

toggles.mergeVariants: Merge spelling variants to the most frequent form
toggles.clipOutliers: Clamp outliers to the Tukey fences

recipe.columnsHint: The settings above are the defaults. A column may override them — a median makes sense for an age and none at all for a postcode.
recipe.unmarked_one: {{count}} column was filled without marking where the blanks were: {{columns}}. A blank field is rarely blank at random — the fact of the blank is often predictive on its own, and filling it silently erases that.
recipe.unmarked_other: {{count}} columns were filled without marking where the blanks were: {{columns}}. A blank field is rarely blank at random — the fact of the blank is often predictive on its own, and filling it silently erases that.

preview.title: Preview
preview.note_one: First row shown — missing cells appear as “—”.
preview.note_other: First {{count}} rows shown — missing cells appear as “—”.

drift.title: Drift check
drift.hint: Compare a new batch against {{name}} (the loaded reference): schema differences, distribution shifts (PSI), new or vanished categories. The new file is parsed in your browser too — nothing is uploaded.
drift.verdict: {{name}} vs the reference: {{drifted}} of {{total}} columns drifted ({{refRows}} → {{newRows}} rows).
drift.note: PSI (Population Stability Index) measures how much a column’s distribution moved, over bins built from the reference. Conventional reading: < 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate, > 0.25 strong — a model trained on the reference should be re-examined.

privacy.title: Nothing leaves your browser
privacy.body: The file is parsed and cleaned inside a Web Worker; the page only ever receives the quality report, counters and a few preview rows. Exports are generated locally, and “Open in the ML Lab” hands the cleaned dataset to the lab in memory — no server is involved at any point, as the strict Content-Security-Policy of this site enforces.

sql.title: Analytical SQL
sql.body: A real analytical SQL engine (DuckDB) running inside your browser, over the file you just loaded — joins, window functions, aggregations, no server. The file is read exactly as you dropped it, before the cleaning recipe: what you query is what you can reopen yourself.
sql.openNote: Downloaded once and then kept by your browser, like the vision models. Nothing goes out: the engine comes from our domain and your data does not leave it.
sql.failed: The SQL engine could not start ({{reason}}). The rest of the Data Studio is unaffected.
sql.tables: Available table: {{tables}} — {{file}} (original file, before the recipe).
sql.noSource: No file attached yet. Add one below.
sql.capNote: The display is capped to stay responsive; the CSV export and the ML Lab handoff carry the rows shown. Add a LIMIT or a filter to frame the result.

ai.title: Deep learning, still in your browser.
ai.lede: Neural modules built on the same rule as the lab: the model comes to your data — never the other way around.

vision.title: Vision playground
vision.description: Classify a photo, find every object and locate faces with three real neural networks on ONNX Runtime Web — running in a Web Worker on your machine.

chat.title: Chat over your data
chat.description: Ask questions in plain French or English — averages, counts with conditions, top N, correlations. A deterministic local interpreter by default, with a real language model available as an option, running in your browser: either way, your data and your questions never leave the machine.

chat.title: Ask your data a question.
chat.lede: Load a dataset and ask in plain French or English: averages, medians, counts under a condition, top N, breakdowns, correlations, missing values. Everything is interpreted and computed right here.

drop.title: Drop a CSV or Excel file
drop.hint: or click to browse — read locally in a Web Worker, never uploaded.

chat.error: This file could not be read. Try a CSV, TSV or Excel file with a header row.
chat.welcome: Ready. Ask a question below, or tap one of the ideas.

answers.scalarPartial: The {{op}} of {{column}} is {{value}} ({{used}} usable values out of {{rows}} rows).
answers.correlation: Pearson correlation between {{a}} and {{b}}: {{value}} over {{rows}} pairs — {{strength}}.

strength.weak: a weak or no linear link

answers.noMissing: No missing cells — this dataset is complete.

chat.unknown: I did not understand that. Ask for an average, a median, a min/max, a sum, a count under a condition, a top N, a breakdown, a correlation or the missing values — naming your columns. I would rather say so than invent an answer.

engine.title: Interpreter
engine.deterministicNote: Instant, always available, same answer every time
engine.llmNote: Qwen3-0.6B, {{size}}, downloaded once — needs WebGPU. Called in as backup when the deterministic interpreter does not understand
engine.noWebgpu: This browser has no WebGPU, so the local model cannot run here — its quantized embedding kernel has no WASM implementation, and there is nothing honest to fall back to at its size. The deterministic interpreter stays fully available.
engine.downloadNote: Downloaded once, then kept by your browser and available offline. Nothing is uploaded: it runs on your machine, on your data — and the deterministic interpreter keeps working whether you download it or not.
engine.readyNote: How the two work together: the deterministic interpreter reads your question first — it can only ever name a column that exists and a value that really occurs in it, so when it understands, nothing overrides it. And it only claims to understand once it has read the WHOLE question: if one word escapes it, it refuses rather than answer a shorter question. The local model then takes over: it only READS your question and turns it into a calculation, it never computes anything itself, so no number ever comes from a language model. If neither manages, you are told so — never an invented answer. The line under each answer says who replied.
engine.failed: The local model could not be loaded ({{reason}}). The deterministic interpreter is unaffected.

by.llm: question read by the local model · computed by the deterministic engine
by.none: the deterministic interpreter did not understand
by.none-both: neither the deterministic interpreter nor the local model understood

engine.constrainedNote: The model writes its query under constraint: at every token, anything outside the query grammar is made impossible to pick. It cannot invent a column, an operator, or a value your column does not hold. It keeps one way of saying no, deliberately: forcing a valid answer would turn « I did not understand » into a wrong number.
engine.unconstrainedNote: Grammar-constrained decoding is unavailable for this model: its answers are still checked before they run, but nothing stops them from being malformed in the first place.

honesty.title: Honest by design
honesty.body: By default this assistant is a deterministic local interpreter — not a language model. It only computes what it fully understands, says so when it does not, and neither your data nor your questions ever leave the browser.
honesty.coming: Since V27 a real language model can be added: Qwen3-0.6B, open weights under Apache-2.0, self-hosted and downloaded only if you accept its 355 MB. It runs entirely on your machine and it never computes an answer — it only translates your question into a query, which the deterministic engine executes. The deterministic interpreter always reads first; the model is called only on the questions it cannot understand, and its translation then passes a closed-grammar check. A note under every answer says which engine produced it — or that neither understood. A generative assistant behind an API would need a server and a secret key that must never ship in a browser — that is the road LabML did not take.

vision.title: What does a neural network see?
vision.lede: Drop a photo: three self-hosted neural networks — an EfficientNet-Lite4 classifier (1,000 classes), a YOLOX-Nano object detector (80 kinds of things) and an UltraFace face detector — run locally through ONNX Runtime Web (WebAssembly). The image never leaves your browser.
vision.loading: Downloading the three models (~19 MB, once — they are then cached, offline included)…
vision.error: The model could not be loaded or run. Reload the page and check your connection for the first download.

drop.title: Drop an image here
drop.hint: or click to browse — JPEG, PNG, WebP… It is processed locally, nothing is uploaded.

webcam.error: Camera unavailable or permission denied — the file drop above still works.

results.title: What the networks see
results.working: The network is looking at your image…
results.empty: The analysis will appear here once you drop an image.
results.note: EfficientNet-Lite4 (77.6 % ImageNet top-1) still always answers with its closest of 1,000 classes — even on an image it does not understand — and its class names stay in English.
results.subject: Main subject — ImageNet top 5

verdict.people_one: A person is in this picture — ImageNet-1k has no class for one.
verdict.people_other: {{count}} people are in this picture — ImageNet-1k has no class for a person.
verdict.peopleWhy: Of its 1,000 labels, 118 name dog breeds and none names a human being. The classifier cannot abstain: it renormalizes over the thousand and returns the nearest, here « {{label}} » at {{p}} %. That is not what the photo shows. The detectors below, which do know about people, are what says so.
verdict.unsureWhy: Below {{floor}} % the top classes are near-ties and naming the winner claims a confidence the network does not have. The five candidates stay listed — read them as a shortlist, not an answer. This bar comes from the fourteen-image bench: no correct answer measured below 70.5 %, no wrong one above 41.2 %. Fourteen images is a narrow base, and the bar is stated so it can be re-measured.

results.objectsNone: No objects detected — nothing above the 35 % confidence bar.
results.detNote: Detection says where, not who: YOLOX-Nano knows the 80 everyday COCO classes (35 % confidence bar), UltraFace only locates faces — neither recognizes anyone, and nothing leaves the tab.

how.title: How it works — and why it is private
how.body: The photo is prepared in canvases (a 224² center crop, a 416² letterbox and a 320×240 frame), then handed to a Web Worker where ONNX Runtime executes the three networks in WebAssembly; the box math — grids, IoU, non-maximum suppression — is hand-written and unit-tested. Models and runtime are served by this site itself: the strict Content-Security-Policy still forbids any third-party call, so the photo cannot leave the tab.
